units.title: Functions
units.summary: Defining, prototyping and calling functions, passing by value and by reference, return values, scope and lifetime, default arguments, overloading, exit(), and stubs and drivers.

lessons.title: Why functions, defining, calling and prototypes
lessons.html:
The idea: give a group of statements a name

A function is a group of statements with a name. You write the statements once. After that, anywhere in the program, you write the name followed by parentheses and those statements run. Doing that is called calling the function. If you know Python, this is the same idea as def. You have already written one function in every program: main.

Why bother? One long main is hard to read, test and fix. Modular programming means splitting a program into small, separate functions, each doing one task. The textbook calls this divide and conquer: solve many small problems instead of one big one. It gives you:

  • Code reuse. Write the statements for a task once, as a function, then call that function wherever the task is needed. A fix made in the function then fixes every place at once.
  • Simpler code. Each function is short, and its name says what it does.
  • Easier testing. You can check one function at a time.
  • Teamwork. Different people can write different functions.

The parts of a function definition

A function definition is the complete function: what it is called and what it does. Here are two. The first prints something and sends nothing back. The second works out a number and sends it back.

void stars()                 // header
{                            // body starts
    cout << "*****" << endl;
}                            // body ends

int cube(int n)              // header
{
    return n * n * n;        // body
}

Every definition has four parts:

  1. The return type: the type of the value the function sends back to the code that called it. cube sends back an int. stars sends back nothing, so its return type is the key word void, which means "no value".
  2. The name. It follows the same rules as a variable name.
  3. The parameter list, in parentheses. A parameter is a variable that receives a value when the function is called. cube has one parameter, int n. Every parameter has its own type. Empty parentheses mean the function takes no values.
  4. The body: the statements between { and }.

The first line, made of the return type, the name and the parameter list, is the function header. There is no semicolon after a header. The body follows it directly. The header and body may share one line: int cube(int n) { return n * n * n; } is still a full definition.

Python never makes you write types. C++ does: the header must state the return type and the type of every parameter. Python's def cube(n): becomes int cube(int n) in C++.

Inside cube, the statement return n * n * n; works out the value and sends it back to the caller. The lesson on return values covers return in full. For now, it is how a function hands back its answer.

Calling a function

A function call is the function's name followed by parentheses that hold the values you are sending. Those values are called arguments. A call has no return type and no types inside the parentheses. Only headers and prototypes (below) contain types.

stars();        // calls stars. A statement on its own.
x = cube(4);    // calls cube, sending the argument 4.
                // cube sends back 64, so x becomes 64.

A void function sends back no value, so its call is a statement on its own. A function with a return type such as int sends back a value, so you use its call where a value is wanted, as in x = cube(4);. When cube finishes, the call is replaced by the value it sent back.

The names in the header never appear in the call. Suppose the header is void showValue(int quantity) and you want to send your variable count. The call is showValue(count);. When it runs, the parameter quantity receives the value of count. The next lesson explains exactly how arguments are matched to parameters.

Even with no arguments, the parentheses are required. stars(); calls the function. stars; only names it, and nothing is printed.

What happens when a function is called

A call is a jump. The program leaves the statement it is on, runs the function's body from the top, and when the body ends it comes back and carries on with the statement after the call. Two more facts:

  • Execution always begins at the first statement of main, wherever main sits in the file. A function written above main does not run first.
  • A function runs only when it is called. A function that is never called never runs, and one that is called twice runs twice.
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void stars()
{
    cout << "*****" << endl;
}

int main()
{
    cout << "Start" << endl;
    stars();
    cout << "Middle" << endl;
    stars();
    cout << "End" << endl;
    return 0;
}

Trace it one statement at a time, starting in main:

Where we areStatementPrints
maincout << "Start"Start
mainstars(); jumps into stars
starscout << "*****"*****
starsreaches }, goes back to main
maincout << "Middle"Middle
mainstars(); jumps into stars again
starscout << "*****"*****
maincout << "End"End

The output is five lines: Start, *****, Middle, *****, End.

Functions that call other functions

Any function can call any other function. Picture each call leaving a bookmark at the spot it jumped from. When a function ends, control goes back to the most recent bookmark: the statement right after the call, in the function that made the call. It does not jump straight back to main.

void inner()
{
    cout << "in inner" << endl;
}

void outer()
{
    cout << "outer starts" << endl;
    inner();
    cout << "outer ends" << endl;
}

int main()
{
    cout << "main starts" << endl;
    outer();
    cout << "main ends" << endl;
    return 0;
}
main    prints "main starts", calls outer   (bookmark in main)
outer   prints "outer starts", calls inner  (bookmark in outer)
inner   prints "in inner", ends: back to the bookmark in outer
outer   prints "outer ends", ends: back to the bookmark in main
main    prints "main ends"

The calls nest like a stack of plates: the last function started is the first to finish. Notice also that inner is defined first but runs second. The order of the definitions in the file does not decide the order things happen. The calls do.

Where definitions go

Every function definition is written on its own at the top level of the file, outside every other function, one after another. A function definition can never be placed inside another function, not even inside main. Python lets you put a def inside a def. C++ does not:

int main()
{
    void stars()            // ERROR: a function definition
    {                       // is not allowed here
        cout << "*****" << endl;
    }
    stars();
    return 0;
}

The compiler reads from the top down: prototypes

The compiler reads your file once, from top to bottom. When it reaches a call, it must already know the function's name, return type and parameter types, so it can check that the call is legal. Python only looks a name up when that line actually runs. C++ checks everything before the program runs, so this program does not compile:

int main()
{
    greet();    // error: 'greet' was not declared in this scope
    return 0;
}

void greet()
{
    cout << "Hi" << endl;
}

greet exists, but further down. At the moment the compiler reads the call, it has never heard of greet. There are two fixes.

  • Fix 1: move the whole definition of greet above main.
  • Fix 2: leave the definition below main and put a function prototype above main.

A prototype is the header with a semicolon on the end and no body. It is also called a function declaration: it announces that the function exists and how to call it. The definition, further down, supplies the body.

void greet(int times);      // prototype: header plus ;

int main()
{
    greet(2);               // fine: the prototype was seen
    return 0;
}

void greet(int times)       // definition: header, no ;
{
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++)
        cout << "Hi" << endl;
}

This prints Hi on two lines. The rules for prototypes:

  • A prototype is the header plus a semicolon.
  • Parameter names are optional in a prototype. The compiler only needs the types to check a call, so void greet(int); is a legal prototype. In the definition's header the names are required, because the body uses them.
  • The prototype and the definition must match: same return type, same name, same number of parameters, same types in the same order.
  • To write a prototype from a description, put the pieces in this order: return type, name, parameter types in parentheses, semicolon. "A function average receives two int values and returns a double" becomes double average(int, int);.

A semicolon after the header of a definition is an error. The semicolon turns the line into a prototype, and the body under it then belongs to nothing:

void greet(int times);   // this ; ends a prototype...
{                        // ...so this block is an error
    cout << "Hi" << endl;
}

Telling the three kinds of line apart

KindExampleReturn type in front?What is in the parenthesesWhat comes after
Prototypeint cube(int n);Yestypes (names optional)a semicolon, no body
Header of a definitionint cube(int n)Yestypes and namesthe body in braces, no semicolon
Callx = cube(4);Novalues only, no typespart of a statement

A quick test: look at what sits directly in front of the function name. No return type there means a call. A return type plus a semicolon at the end means a prototype. A return type plus a body means a definition. Careful with a line such as int a = cube(4);. The int belongs to the new variable a, not to cube. Nothing sits in front of cube but =, and the parentheses hold a value, so the line contains a call.

void functions

If a function does not return a value, the key word void is written as its return type. A void function does its job, such as printing, and ends when it reaches its closing brace. It does not need a return statement. It may use return;, with no value, to leave early. Its call cannot be used as a value: x = stars(); does not compile, because there is nothing to store.

Mistakes students make

  • Putting a semicolon after the header of a definition.
  • Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a prototype. Without it, the line is a header.
  • Writing types in a call: showValue(int count); does not compile. Write showValue(count);.
  • Writing the parameter's name in the call instead of the variable you want to send.
  • Calling a function above its definition with no prototype. The error is "not declared in this scope".
  • Writing a function definition inside main.
  • Thinking the program starts at the first function in the file. It starts at main.
  • Thinking a finished function always goes back to main. It goes back to whichever function called it.
  • Leaving the parentheses off a call: stars; does nothing.

What to remember for the test

  • Modular programming (divide and conquer): small functions, one task each. Code reuse: write once, call many times.
  • Definition = header + body. Header = return type, name, parameter list, no semicolon.
  • Prototype = header + semicolon, no body. Parameter names are optional. Also called a function declaration.
  • Call = name + arguments in parentheses. No return type, no types.
  • void means the function returns no value. Call it as a statement on its own.
  • Execution starts at the first statement of main. A function runs only when called.
  • A function returns to the statement after its call, in whichever function made the call.
  • The compiler must see a prototype or the definition before the first call.
  • Never define a function inside another function.
  • For "what does this print" questions, start in main and follow each call into the function and back out.

lessons.title: Arguments, parameters and passing by value
lessons.html:
The one idea: a call copies values into new variables

When a function is called, C++ creates each of its parameters as a brand-new variable and fills it with a copy of the value in the matching spot of the call. Only then does the body run. So for a function that starts void show(int n), the call show(7) behaves as if the body began with the line int n = 7;.

Hold on to that picture: "each parameter is a new variable, set from its argument, like int n = 7;". It explains every rule in this lesson: how values are matched, what happens when the types differ, and why the function cannot change the caller's variables.

Parameters and arguments

Two words that are easy to mix up:

  • A parameter is a variable declared in the parentheses of a function header. It receives a value when the function is called. Some books call it a formal parameter or formal argument.
  • An argument is a value written in the parentheses of a call. It is the value being sent. Some books call it an actual argument or actual parameter.

Memory aid: the parameter is the placeholder in the definition. The argument is the actual value at the call.

void showArea(double len, int wid)  // len and wid: parameters
{
    cout << len * wid << endl;
}
...
showArea(2.5, 4);           // 2.5 and 4: arguments
showArea(x + 1.0, n * 2);   // arguments can be expressions

An argument can be a literal such as 4, a variable such as count, or any expression such as n * 2. C++ works the expression out first and passes only its value. If x is 2.0 and n is 3, the second call is the same as showArea(3.0, 6), and it prints 18.

Arguments are matched by position

The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on, left to right. Names play no part. A variable in the call does not look for a parameter with the same name. Python lets you write f(bottom=20) to choose a parameter by name. C++ has no such thing.

void showQuotient(int top, int bottom)
{
    cout << top / bottom << endl;
}

int top = 4, bottom = 20;
showQuotient(bottom, top);   // parameter top = 20, bottom = 4
                             // prints 20 / 4, which is 5
showQuotient(top, bottom);   // parameter top = 4, bottom = 20
                             // prints 4 / 20, which is 0

In the first call, main's bottom (20) is written first, so it goes into the parameter called top. The matching names are a coincidence that C++ ignores. (The second call prints 0 because / between two int values is integer division and drops the fraction.)

Because matching is by position, a call must supply exactly one argument for each parameter, in order. Given void label(int row, int col, char mark);:

label(1, 2, '#');           // legal: three values, right order
label(1, 2);                // error: too few arguments
label(1, 2, '#', 4);        // error: too many arguments
label(int 1, int 2, '#');   // error: no types in a call

There is one exception to "exactly one argument for each parameter": a parameter can be given a default argument, a value that is used when the caller leaves that argument out. A later lesson covers that. A parameter without a default must always receive an argument.

Every parameter needs its own type

When you define ordinary variables, one type can cover several names: int a, b, c;. A parameter list does not allow that. Each parameter needs its own type in front of its name.

int addUp(int a, b, c)           // error: b and c have no type
int addUp(int a, int b, int c)   // correct

Parameters are separated by commas, and a function may have as many as it needs.

When the argument's type differs from the parameter's

Go back to the picture: the parameter is set from the argument, like a definition with an initial value. So the value is converted to the parameter's type, exactly as int whole = 9.99; would convert it. The parameter keeps the type written in the header, whatever you pass.

ArgumentParameter typeWhat the parameter holds
a double such as 9.99int9. The fraction is dropped. This is truncation, not rounding: 9.99 does not become 10, and -2.5 becomes -2.
an int such as 6double6.0
an int such as 67charthe character whose code is 67, which is 'C'
a char such as 'A'intits code, 65

Two facts make these rows clear:

  • Every char is stored as a number code. In the code table most systems use (ASCII), 'A' is 65, 'B' 66, 'C' 67, and 'a' is 97, 'b' 98. When a char is used in arithmetic, C++ uses its code, so 'a' + 1 is the int 98. Store 98 in a char and it is 'b' again. cout prints a char variable as a character and an int as a number.
  • cout prints a whole-number double without a decimal point. A double holding 6.0 prints as 6. (Use fixed with setprecision when you want the zeros to show.)
void report(int whole, double exact)
{
    cout << whole << " and " << exact << endl;
}
void repeat(char ch, int times)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++)
        cout << ch;
    cout << endl;
}

report(9.99, 9.99);   // whole = 9, exact = 9.99:  9 and 9.99
report(-2.5, 6);      // whole = -2, exact = 6.0:  -2 and 6
repeat('#', 4);       // ch = '#', times = 4:      ####
repeat('A' + 2, 3);   // 'A' + 2 is 67, ch = 'C':  CCC

This compiles. A double passed to an int parameter is legal C++, even though part of the value is lost. Python never converts like this: a Python parameter simply holds whatever you pass. In C++ the header decides the type.

Passing by value: the parameter is a copy

Everything so far is called passing by value, and it is what C++ does by default, for every parameter written without an &. The parameter is a separate variable with its own memory location. It starts with a copy of the argument's value, and after that the two have nothing to do with each other. Changing the parameter never changes the caller's variable, even when the two have the same name.

void triple(int n)
{
    n = n * 3;
    cout << "inside: " << n << endl;
}
int main()
{
    int n = 4;
    triple(n);
    cout << "main: " << n << endl;
    return 0;
}

There are two variables called n here, one in each function. Track both:

Statementmain's ntriple's nPrints
int n = 4;4does not exist yet
triple(n); starts44, a copy
n = n * 3;412
cout in triple412inside: 12
triple ends4destroyed
cout in main4main: 4

Python behaves the same way if a function gives one of its parameters a new value: the caller's variable does not change.

The classic example is a swap function written with value parameters:

void swapVals(int first, int second)
{
    int temp = first;
    first = second;
    second = temp;
}

int p = 8, q = 3;
swapVals(p, q);
cout << p << " " << q;     // prints 8 3
call starts      first = 8, second = 3   (copies of p and q)
temp = first     temp = 8
first = second   first = 3
second = temp    second = 8              the copies are swapped
function ends    first, second, temp destroyed
back in main     p = 8, q = 3            never touched

The swap really happened, but only to the copies, and they are thrown away when the function ends.

Why pass by value? It is safe. The function cannot damage the caller's data by accident, because it only ever sees a copy. The cost is that the function cannot send results back through its parameters.

When a function must change the caller's variable

Then it needs a reference parameter, written with & after the type: void triple(int& n). A reference parameter is not a copy. It is another name for the caller's variable, so changing it changes the original. The lesson on reference parameters covers this.

So the rule runs both ways. To make sure a function cannot change the caller's variable, pass by value: an ordinary parameter with no &. Two things that do not help:

  • Giving the parameter the same name as the caller's variable. They are still two separate variables, as the triple trace shows.
  • Making the variable global, meaning defined outside every function. Every function can then see and change it, which removes protection instead of adding it. The lesson on local and global variables explains globals.

Parameters live only while their function runs

A variable's scope is the part of the program where its name can be used. A parameter's scope is the body of its own function. It is created when the call starts, holding the copied value, and destroyed when the function returns. A later call gets brand-new parameters.

So after triple(x); returns, main cannot use triple's parameter. Writing cout << n; in a main that has no n of its own is a compile error: "n was not declared in this scope". To get a result out of a function, return it or use a reference parameter.

Mistakes students make

  • Calling the variable in the header an argument. In the header it is a parameter. In the call it is an argument.
  • Thinking arguments are matched to parameters by name. They are matched by position only.
  • Writing int a, b in a parameter list. Each parameter needs its own type: int a, int b.
  • Writing types in a call, or passing too few or too many arguments.
  • Rounding when a double goes into an int parameter. The fraction is dropped: 3.9 becomes 3.
  • Expecting cout to print 6.0 for a double holding 6. It prints 6.
  • Thinking a function changed the caller's variable because it changed its parameter. With pass by value only the copy changes.
  • Thinking the same name links two variables in different functions. It never does.
  • Using a parameter in main after the call. It no longer exists.

What to remember for the test

  • Parameter (formal parameter): the variable in the header. Argument (actual argument): the value in the call.
  • At the call, each parameter is a new variable set from its argument, like int n = 7;.
  • Arguments match parameters by position, one for one, unless a default argument fills a gap.
  • Any expression can be an argument. Its value is passed.
  • Each parameter needs its own type: int a, int b.
  • The argument is converted to the parameter's type. Double to int truncates. Int to char gives the character with that code.
  • Pass by value is the default: the parameter is a copy in its own memory, so the caller's variable cannot change.
  • A by-value swap swaps only the copies. Changing the caller's variable needs a reference parameter (&).
  • A parameter exists only while its function runs, and only that function can use its name.
  • For output questions, write each call as a list of parameter = value assignments, then trace the body.

lessons.title: The return statement and returning values
lessons.html:
The idea: a function can hand back an answer

The void functions so far did a job, such as printing, and sent nothing back. A value-returning function works something out and sends one value back to the statement that called it. You have used these already: pow(2.0, 3.0) hands back 8, and sqrt(25.0) hands back 5.

The picture to hold: when the function finishes, its call is replaced by the value it returned. y = pow(2.0, 3.0) + 1; becomes y = 8 + 1;. Python works the same way with return. The difference is that in C++ the header must say what type of value comes back.

Writing a value-returning function

int square(int n)     // return type int: sends back an int
{
    return n * n;
}

The return type is anything other than void. The statement return expression; works out the expression, ends the function, and sends the value back. To write a header from a description, go in order: return type, name, then each parameter with its own type. "A function maxOf that receives two doubles x and y and returns a double" gives double maxOf(double x, double y).

A good function does one task, and its name says which: getScore, isLeapYear, square.

Using the returned value

A call to a value-returning function can go anywhere a value of that type can go: on the right of =, in cout, in arithmetic, as an argument to another call, or in a condition.

int a = square(4);                 // a is 16
result = square(6);                // stores 36 in existing result
cout << square(2) + square(5);     // 4 + 25: prints 29
cout << square(square(3));         // prints 81 (see below)
if (square(x) > 50)                // a call inside a condition

For a call inside a call, work from the inside out. The inner call runs first, and its result becomes the argument of the outer call:

square(square(3))
inner: square(3) returns 9
outer: square(9) returns 81

To store a result in a variable that already exists, put the call on the right of = with no type in front: result = square(6);. You may also ignore a returned value. square(4); on its own line compiles, and the 16 is simply thrown away.

return ends the function at once

The moment a return statement runs, the function is over. Any statements after it are skipped, and the value goes back to the caller. A function may contain several return statements, but each call runs only one of them.

int sign(int n)
{
    if (n < 0)
        return -1;
    if (n == 0)
        return 0;
    return 1;
}
sign(-5)   n < 0 is true: return -1. The function ends here.
sign(0)    n < 0 false, n == 0 true: return 0.
sign(8)    both tests false: reaches return 1.

Three things return does not do:

  • It does not print anything. A returned value appears on screen only if the caller sends it to cout.
  • It does not end the program. It ends only the current function, and the caller carries on.
  • It cannot send back two values. A function returns at most one value per call. return x, y; compiles (g++ may warn), but it returns only y. To give back several results, a function uses reference parameters (a later lesson).

The returned value is converted to the return type

Just as an argument is converted to its parameter's type, the value in a return is converted to the return type in the header before it leaves the function. This causes two classic traps.

Trap 1: integer division happens before the conversion.

double average2(int a, int b)
{
    return (a + b) / 2;     // int / int
}

average2(5, 8):
(a + b) / 2     13 / 2 is integer division: 6
return 6        converted to the return type: 6.0
cout            prints 6

The double return type comes too late: the .5 was lost in the division. Write (a + b) / 2.0 and the function returns 6.5.

Trap 2: an int return type cuts the fraction off inside the function.

int third(double x)
{
    return x / 3;           // 10.0 / 3 is 3.333...
}

double d = third(10.0);     // third returns the int 3,
                            // so d is 3.0 and prints as 3

Storing the result in a double cannot bring the fraction back, because it was dropped before the value left third. And the conversion truncates: a function declared int that computes 4.9 returns 4, not 5.

A second conversion can happen at the receiving end. Suppose a function average returns the double 6.5. Then int k = average(5, 8); stores 6 in k, because an int variable cannot hold the fraction. So for any output question, apply the conversions in order: first to the return type, then to the type of the variable that stores the result.

Every path must reach a return

A value-returning function must run a return with a value on every path through it. Look at this one:

int larger(int a, int b)
{
    if (a > b)
        return a;
}          // if a <= b, nothing is returned

When a is not bigger, the function reaches its closing brace with no value to send back. g++ only gives a warning ("control reaches end of non-void function"), so the program still builds. But it is broken: the C++ rules say the behaviour is undefined, which means the caller may get a meaningless value, or something worse. Treat that warning as an error. The fix is to make sure every path returns: add return b; before the closing brace.

Questions that show a broken function often hide a second trap beside a missing return: operator precedence. / is done before +, so a + b + c / 3 means a + b + (c / 3). With 4, 5 and 6 that is 4 + 5 + 2 = 11, not the average 5. Write (a + b + c) / 3.0.

void functions and return

A void function returns nothing. It may use return; with no value to leave early. It may not return a value: return n * n * n; inside a void function is a compile error ("return-statement with a value, in function returning void"). If the function must send a value back, change its return type.

void showRatio(int a, int b)
{
    if (b == 0)
    {
        cout << "cannot divide" << endl;
        return;                 // leave now
    }
    cout << a / b << endl;
}

showRatio(9, 0);   // prints cannot divide, then return; ends it
showRatio(9, 3);   // the if is skipped: prints 3

Returning a bool

A function that answers a yes or no question returns bool. A comparison already has the value true or false, so you can return it directly, with no if needed. Name such functions like a question.

bool isEven(int n)
{
    return n % 2 == 0;     // true when n divides by 2
}

if (isEven(10))            // correct: call it in the condition
    cout << "even";
cout << isEven(10) << isEven(7);   // prints 10

cout prints true as 1 and false as 0, not as words. So isEven(10) prints 1 and isEven(7) prints 0, and with nothing between them the output is 10.

Three wrong ways to use it in an if:

  • if (isEven) names the function without calling it. No argument is passed and the function never runs. C++ treats a function's name in a condition as true, so this test is always true. g++ only warns.
  • if (bool isEven(n)) and if (isEven(int n)) put types inside a call. Neither compiles.

Menu-driven programs and hierarchy charts

A menu-driven program shows a list of choices, reads the user's choice, does what was picked, and repeats until the user picks Quit. Functions fit this well: a loop reads the choice, and a switch calls one function per choice. The default case catches choices that match no case.

void showMenu()
{
    cout << "1 Area  2 Perimeter  3 Quit" << endl;
}
int area(int w, int h)      { return w * h; }
int perimeter(int w, int h) { return 2 * (w + h); }

int main()
{
    int choice;
    do
    {
        showMenu();
        cin >> choice;
        switch (choice)
        {
            case 1:  cout << area(4, 5) << endl;      break;
            case 2:  cout << perimeter(4, 5) << endl; break;
            case 3:  break;
            default: cout << "Invalid" << endl;
        }
    } while (choice != 3);
    return 0;
}

If the user types 2, 7, 1, 3, each pass prints the menu line and then:

Choice readWhat runsPrints after the menu
2perimeter(4, 5) returns 1818
7no case 7, so defaultInvalid
1area(4, 5) returns 2020
3case 3: break;nothing. choice != 3 is false, so the loop ends

Note that break inside a switch leaves only the switch, not the loop. The loop ends because its condition becomes false.

Before writing a program like this, programmers plan it with a hierarchy chart: a tree of boxes with main at the top and, under each function, the functions it calls. For this program:

                 main
       ___________|___________
      |           |           |
  showMenu      area      perimeter

If area called another function, that function would sit in a box under area. A hierarchy chart shows only the structure: which function calls which. It does not show the order of statements, decisions or loops. That is the job of a flowchart, which draws the step-by-step logic with diamonds for decisions.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing return value; in a void function. Change the return type instead.
  • Forgetting the return in a value-returning function, or missing it on one path.
  • Expecting a double return type to rescue integer division. (a + b) / 2 with int values has already lost the fraction.
  • Expecting an int function to return 3.5, or to round 4.9 up. It truncates to 3 and 4.
  • Thinking return prints its value or ends the program.
  • Trying to return two values with one return.
  • Writing if (isEven) instead of if (isEven(n)).
  • Expecting cout << isEven(4); to print the word true. It prints 1.
  • Writing int result = cube(4); when result already exists. Write result = cube(4);.

What to remember for the test

  • A value-returning function has a return type other than void and sends back one value with return expression;.
  • The call is replaced by the returned value, so it can go wherever a value can go. Nested calls run inside out.
  • return ends the function immediately. Lines after it do not run.
  • The returned value is converted to the return type, then to the type of the variable that stores it. Double to int truncates.
  • Watch for integer division and for / being done before +.
  • Every path of a value-returning function must return a value. Missing it is only a warning in g++, but the result is undefined.
  • A void function may use return; to leave early, never return value;.
  • A bool function is called inside a condition: if (isPrime(n)). cout prints true as 1, false as 0.
  • Menu-driven program: loop, read choice, switch calls one function per choice, default for bad input.
  • Hierarchy chart: which function calls which. Flowchart: the step-by-step logic.

lessons.title: Local, global and static local variables
lessons.html:
Two questions about every variable

Once a program has several functions, you need to ask two separate questions about each variable:

  • Scope: where in the program can its name be used?
  • Lifetime: when does it exist? That is the period from when the variable is created in memory until it is destroyed.

They are different ideas. A variable can have a small scope and a long lifetime, as you will see with static. This lesson covers three kinds of variable: ordinary local, global and static local. For each one, ask: where can I use it, how long does it live, and what does it hold if I never give it a value?

Local variables

A local variable is one you define inside the body of a function. Parameters are local variables too. Its scope is its own function only, from the line where it is defined to the end of the block (the { }) that holds it. No other function can use its name:

void setUp()
{
    int score = 10;      // local to setUp
}
void report()
{
    cout << score;       // error: 'score' was not declared
}                        //        in this scope

report cannot see inside setUp. If report needs the value, it must receive it as a parameter, or setUp must return it.

Because the scope is so small, two different functions may each have a local variable with the same name. Two variables called total in two functions are two separate variables that never clash, just as two people named Sam in two different houses are different people.

Inside one function it is different. A parameter belongs to the function's body, so the body cannot define another variable with the same name:

void f(int n)
{
    int n = 2;     // error: declaration of 'int n'
}                  //        shadows a parameter

Lifetime of an ordinary local: it is created when the function runs its definition and destroyed when the function returns. The next call creates a brand-new variable. So an ordinary local cannot remember anything from one call to the next:

void countVisits()
{
    int visits = 0;      // a new visits, set to 0, every call
    visits++;
    cout << visits << endl;
}
// called three times, it prints 1, 1, 1

Starting value: an ordinary local that is defined without a value, such as int sum;, is not set to 0. It holds garbage: an unpredictable leftover value from whatever used that memory before. Using it before you assign a value is a bug, and the C++ rules call reading it undefined. Always give locals a starting value: int sum = 0;.

Global variables

A global variable is defined outside every function, usually near the top of the file. Its scope runs from its definition to the end of the file, so every function written below it can read it and change it. Its lifetime is the whole run of the program. If you give it no value, it starts at 0: C++ sets globals to zero before main begins.

int stock = 3;             // global

void addFive()
{
    stock = stock + 5;     // no type: this changes the global
}
int main()
{
    addFive();             // stock: 3 to 8
    addFive();             // stock: 8 to 13
    cout << stock;         // prints 13
    return 0;
}

If you know Python, note the difference: a Python function needs the global key word before it can change a global. A C++ function needs nothing. Any function below the definition can change the global just by assigning to it.

"From its definition to the end of the file" matters. A function written above the global's definition cannot see it at all, because the compiler reads from the top down:

void showLimit()
{
    cout << limit;     // error: 'limit' was not declared
}                      //        in this scope
int limit = 30;        // defined too late for showLimit

This is a compile error, not a run that prints 0 or 30. Moving int limit = 30; above showLimit fixes it.

Why global variables are discouraged

Globals look convenient, since every function can reach them. That is exactly the problem:

  • Bugs are hard to trace. Any function can change a global, so when it holds a wrong value, the culprit could be any function in the program.
  • Functions become hard to reuse. A function that depends on a global cannot be copied into another program without bringing the global along.
  • Programs are harder to test, because a function's result depends on more than its parameters.

The better habit: pass data in through parameters and send results out with return. Then each function is self-contained.

Global constants are the accepted exception. const double TAX_RATE = 0.07; written outside all functions can be used by every function, and it is safe, because no function can change it. The risk with globals is unwanted changes, and a const cannot be changed: TAX_RATE = 0.5; inside a function is a compile error ("assignment of read-only variable"). A constant must be given its value where it is defined.

Shadowing: a local with the same name as a global

What if a function defines a local variable, or has a parameter, with the same name as a global? Inside that function, the name means the local one. The local shadows the global, which means it hides it. Every use of the name in that function refers to the local, and the global is untouched. Outside that function, the name means the global again.

int points = 50;           // global

void bonus()
{
    int points = 7;        // a new local: shadows the global
    points = points * 2;   // changes the local
    cout << points << endl;
}
int main()
{
    bonus();
    cout << points << endl;
    return 0;
}
Statementglobal pointslocal pointsPrints
start of program50does not exist
int points = 7; in bonus507
points = points * 2;5014
cout in bonus501414
bonus returns50destroyed
cout in main5050

The key is the type in front. int points = 7; defines a new local variable. Without the type, points = 7; would be an assignment to the global, and main would then print 14.

Static local variables

Sometimes a function needs to remember something between calls, such as how many times it has been called. A global could do it, but then every function could change it. The answer is a static local variable: put the key word static in front of a local definition.

  • Its scope is still only its own function. Other functions cannot use its name.
  • Its lifetime is the whole run of the program. It is not destroyed when the function returns, so it keeps its value between calls.
  • It is created and initialized once, the first time execution reaches its definition. On later calls the initializer is skipped.
  • If you give it no value, it starts at 0, like a global.
void visit()
{
    int fresh = 10;          // ordinary: re-created every call
    static int total = 10;   // static: set to 10 only once
    fresh += 5;
    total += 5;
    cout << fresh << " " << total << endl;
}

Called three times, it prints:

Callfresh at starttotal at startPrints
1st10 (new)10 (initialized now)15 15
2nd10 (new again)15 (kept, initializer skipped)15 20
3rd10 (new again)20 (kept)15 25

fresh is born at 10 and dies at the end of every call, so it always prints 15. total is set to 10 only on the first call. After that, the line static int total = 10; does nothing, and total carries on from where it was.

Summary table

KindScope: where the name worksLifetimeIf not initialized
Ordinary local (and parameter)its own function, from its definition onone call: created when defined, destroyed on returngarbage
static localits own functionwhole run, initialized once0
Globalfrom its definition to the end of the filewhole run0
Global constantfrom its definition to the end of the filewhole runnot allowed: must be given a value

Mistakes students make

  • Using a local variable of one function inside another function.
  • Assuming an uninitialized local starts at 0. Only globals and statics do.
  • Expecting an ordinary local to remember its value from the last call. Use static.
  • Thinking the initializer of a static local runs on every call. It runs once.
  • Thinking a static local is global. Other functions still cannot use its name.
  • Reading int total = 5; inside a function as a change to the global total. With the type, it is a new local that shadows the global.
  • Using a global in a function written above the global's definition.
  • Defining a local with the same name as a parameter of the same function.
  • Confusing scope (where) with lifetime (when).

What to remember for the test

  • Scope: where a name can be used. Lifetime: how long the variable exists.
  • A local is visible only in its own function. Different functions may reuse the same local name.
  • An ordinary local lives for one call and starts with garbage if not initialized.
  • A global lives for the whole run, starts at 0, and is visible from its definition to the end of the file.
  • Globals are discouraged: any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace and functions are hard to reuse. Global constants are fine.
  • A local or parameter with the same name as a global shadows (hides) it inside that function.
  • static local: initialized once, keeps its value between calls, starts at 0, still visible only in its function.
  • For output questions, keep one column per variable, and remember which ones are new on every call.

lessons.title: Default arguments and reference parameters
lessons.html:
Two tools in this lesson

This lesson adds two tools to the parameter list. Default arguments let a caller leave some arguments out. Reference parameters let a function change the caller's variables. Both are written in the parameter list of the function, never in the call. Exactly where each one goes (prototype, header or both) is different for the two tools, and is covered below.

Default arguments

A default argument is a value written into the parameter list with =. When a call leaves that argument out, the parameter gets the default instead. Python has the same idea: def line(ch="-", length=5):.

void line(char ch = '-', int len = 5)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
        cout << ch;
    cout << endl;
}

line();          // ch = '-', len = 5    prints -----
line('*');       // ch = '*', len = 5    prints *****
line('=', 3);    // ch = '=', len = 3    prints ===

The rule from the last lesson still holds: arguments fill parameters from the left, by position. A default only fills a parameter that no argument reached. So line('*') puts '*' into ch, the first parameter, and len takes its default. Once a call supplies a value, the default for that parameter is ignored.

The rules for default arguments

1. Defaults go at the right-hand end. Once a parameter has a default, every parameter to its right must have one too.

void pack(int a, int b = 2, int c = 3);   // legal
void pack(int a = 1, int b, int c = 3);   // error: b has none

Why: arguments fill from the left, so the only arguments a caller can leave out are the last ones. In the second line there would be no way to give b a value while leaving a out. Python has the same rule.

2. A call can leave out only arguments at the end. It cannot skip one in the middle. Given void pay(double hours, double rate = 15.0, int bonus = 0);:

pay(40);            // rate 15.0, bonus 0
pay(40, 20.0);      // bonus 0
pay(40, 20.0, 50);  // no defaults used
pay(40, , 50);      // syntax error: no gaps allowed
pay();              // error: hours has no default

To give bonus a value, you must also give rate one, even if it is the same 15.0. And a parameter without a default must always receive an argument.

3. Put the default in the prototype if there is one, and only there. If there is no prototype, put it in the header of the definition.

void pay(double hours, double rate = 15.0, int bonus = 0);

int main()
{
    pay(40);       // the compiler knows the defaults
    return 0;
}

void pay(double hours, double rate, int bonus)  // no defaults
{
    cout << hours * rate + bonus << endl;
}

Repeating the default in the header is a compile error ("default argument given for parameter 2"), even with the same value. Putting it only in the header fails too: the compiler checks pay(40) in main against the prototype, which it has already read, and the prototype says pay needs more arguments. The error is "too few arguments".

4. What a default can be. Usually a literal such as 10 or a named constant such as LIMIT. An expression built from constants, such as LIMIT * 2, is also fine. A default may never use another parameter of the same function: void f(int a, int b = a); does not compile.

Reference parameters: the idea

Recall pass by value: the parameter is a new variable holding a copy, so the function cannot change the caller's variable. Sometimes that is exactly what you need to do: swap two variables, read input into the caller's variable, or give back more than one result.

A reference variable is another name, an alias, for a variable that already exists. Put & after the type in a parameter to make it a reference parameter. The parameter is then not a new variable with a copy. It is a second name for the caller's variable: one box in memory with two name tags on it. Whatever the function does to the parameter, it does to the caller's variable. This is called passing by reference.

void doubleIt(int& n)     // n will be another name
{                         // for whatever variable is passed
    n = n * 2;
}
int main()
{
    int score = 6;
    doubleIt(score);      // during this call, n IS score
    cout << score;        // prints 12
    return 0;
}
void f(int n) by valuevoid f(int& n) by reference
What n isa new variable holding a copyanother name for the caller's variable
Boxes in memorytwoone
Does n = 99; change the caller's variable?noyes
Can the argument be 5 or x + 1?yesno, it must be a variable

Python has nothing like this for numbers: to get a new number out of a Python function, you return it. In C++ a reference parameter lets the function change the caller's int directly.

Now the swap from the by-value lesson works:

void swapInts(int& a, int& b)
{
    int temp = a;   // keep the old a
    a = b;
    b = temp;
}

int m = 4, k = 9;
swapInts(m, k);      // a is m, b is k
// temp = a: temp = 4
// a = b:    m = 9
// b = temp: k = 4
cout << m << " " << k;   // prints 9 4

The function body is the same as the failed version. The only change is the two & in the header.

Where the & goes, and where it does not

Place& written?Example
Prototypeyesvoid doubleIt(int&); (name optional)
Header of the definitionyesvoid doubleIt(int& n)
The callnodoubleIt(score);
Using the parameter in the bodynon = n * 2; or cin >> n;
  • The & goes after the type and before the name. int& n, int &n and int & n all mean the same: spaces do not matter. int n& is an error.
  • A call to a function with reference parameters looks exactly like a call by value. Only the prototype and header show the difference. Writing doubleIt(&score) means something else (the address of score, a later topic) and does not compile here.
  • Inside the body the parameter is used like any variable, with no &.
  • The argument must be a variable. doubleIt(5) and doubleIt(score + 1) do not compile. There is no variable for n to be another name for, and the function intends to change it. g++ says "cannot bind non-const lvalue reference". An lvalue is something that has a storage place you can assign to, such as a variable.

Mixing value and reference parameters

Each parameter is decided on its own. Only those with & are aliases. Trace carefully, because the alias points to whichever variable is passed in that call:

void scale(int factor, int& target)
{
    target = target * factor;
    factor = 0;            // changes only the copy
}

int u = 3, v = 5;
scale(u, v);
scale(v, u);
Callfactor (copy)target isAfter the call
scale(u, v)copy of u: 3vv = 5 * 3 = 15, u still 3
scale(v, u)copy of v: 15uu = 3 * 15 = 45, v still 15

Setting factor to 0 has no effect outside: it is a copy. In the second call the arguments are swapped, so target is now another name for u, and u is the one that changes.

What reference parameters are used for

Giving back more than one result. return sends back only one value. To send back two, pass the result variables by reference. Inputs that are only read stay by value.

void splitTime(int totalSec, int& minutes, int& seconds)
{
    minutes = totalSec / 60;
    seconds = totalSec % 60;
}

int mins, secs;
splitTime(135, mins, secs);   // mins is 2, secs is 15

Reading input into the caller's variable. A function can read and check a value, and the caller ends up holding it:

void getPositive(int& num)
{
    cin >> num;
    while (num <= 0)
    {
        cout << "Must be positive" << endl;
        cin >> num;
    }
}

If main calls getPositive(n); and the user types -3, 0, 8, the function prints "Must be positive" twice, and n ends up 8. With int num and no &, the 8 would go into a copy, and n would never change.

Combining with a default. A reference parameter can be followed by a parameter with a default, as long as the defaults stay at the right-hand end:

void addPoints(int& score, int points = 10)
{
    score += points;
}

int s = 0;
addPoints(s);      // points = 10: s is 10
addPoints(s, 3);   // points = 3:  s is 13

When to use which: pass by value when the function only needs to read the data, so it cannot damage it by accident. Pass by reference when the function must change the caller's variable or hand back more than one result.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing the default in both the prototype and the header.
  • Giving a parameter a default while a parameter to its right has none.
  • Trying to skip a middle argument, as in pay(40, , 50).
  • Using another parameter as a default: int b = a.
  • Writing & in the call, or when using the parameter in the body.
  • Writing int n& instead of int& n.
  • Forgetting the & in the prototype while writing it in the header. They must match.
  • Passing a literal or an expression to a reference parameter.
  • Assuming every parameter of a function is a reference because one is.
  • Forgetting that in a second call with different arguments the reference refers to a different variable.

What to remember for the test

  • A default argument is used only when its argument is missing. Arguments still fill from the left.
  • Defaults go at the right end of the list. Calls can omit only trailing arguments, never a middle one.
  • Put defaults in the prototype if there is one, otherwise in the header. Never both.
  • A default may be a literal, a named constant, or an expression of constants. Never another parameter.
  • A reference parameter (int& n) is another name for the caller's variable. No copy is made, so changes reach the caller.
  • The & goes after the type in the prototype and header. Not in the call, not in the body. Spaces around it do not matter.
  • The argument for a reference parameter must be a variable.
  • Use references to change the caller's variable or to give back several results, such as a quotient and a remainder.
  • For output questions, write next to each parameter either "copy of x" or "is x", then trace.

lessons.title: Overloading, exit(), stubs and drivers
lessons.html:
Overloading: one name, several functions

Suppose you want a function that gives the larger of two numbers. For int values it should return an int. For double values it should return a double. You could invent two names, largerInt and largerDouble, but C++ lets you use one name for both. Functions that share a name but have different parameter lists are called overloaded functions. Each version does a similar job for different data.

int larger(int a, int b)
{
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}
double larger(double a, double b)
{
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}
int larger(int a, int b, int c)
{
    return larger(larger(a, b), c);
}

(a > b) ? a : b is the conditional operator from the decisions unit: it gives a when a > b is true, otherwise b. Python writes the same thing as a if a > b else b.

At each call, the compiler looks at the arguments, how many there are and what type each one is, and picks the version whose parameter list matches:

larger(3, 8)       two ints     larger(int, int)        8
larger(2.5, 1.5)   two doubles  larger(double, double)  2.5
larger(4, 9, 6)    three ints   larger(int, int, int)   9

To read the type of a literal argument: a whole number such as 5 is an int, a number with a decimal point such as 2.5 is a double, and a character in single quotes such as 'z' is a char.

Python has nothing like this. If a Python file defines def larger twice, the second definition simply replaces the first. C++ keeps every version and chooses between them at each call.

The signature

A function's signature is its name plus the types of its parameters, in order. The signature of double larger(double a, double b) is larger(double, double). Two things are not part of the signature:

  • The return type.
  • The parameter names.

Every function in a program must have a different signature. So overloaded versions must differ in their parameter lists:

Two versions of f differ in...ExampleLegal overloads?
the number of parametersf(int) and f(int, int)yes
the type of a parameterf(int) and f(double)yes
the order of the typesf(int, double) and f(double, int)yes
only the return typeint f() and double f()no
only the parameter namesf(int a) and f(int b)no, same function twice

Why the return type is not enough: the compiler chooses a version from the call, and a call such as getValue() says nothing about what type you want back. The returned value might even be ignored. So int getValue(); and double getValue(); in one program do not compile.

When no version matches exactly

The compiler first looks for a version whose parameter types match the arguments exactly. If there is none, it tries converting the arguments. If exactly one version is the best fit, that one is used. For example, with only void code(int n) available, code('A') converts the char to its code and runs with n equal to 65.

If two versions fit equally well, the call is ambiguous and does not compile. With the two-parameter versions of larger above, larger(3, 2.5) is ambiguous: the int version needs 2.5 converted, the double version needs 3 converted, and neither is better. g++ says "call of overloaded larger(int, double) is ambiguous". The fix is to make the arguments the same type, as in larger(3.0, 2.5).

The exit() function

return ends only the current function, and the caller carries on. Sometimes a program hits an error so serious that it must stop completely, even from deep inside a chain of calls. For that, C++ has exit, from the header <cstdlib>. Python programmers know it as sys.exit().

exit(n); ends the whole program immediately, from any function. Nothing else runs: not the rest of that function, not the rest of the function that called it, not the rest of main.

#include <iostream>
#include <cstdlib>
using namespace std;

void checkAge(int age)
{
    if (age < 0)
    {
        cout << "Bad age" << endl;
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);     // the whole program ends here
    }
    cout << "Age ok" << endl;
}
void process(int age)
{
    checkAge(age);
    cout << "Processed" << endl;
}
int main()
{
    process(30);
    process(-4);
    cout << "Done" << endl;
    return 0;
}
process(30)   checkAge(30): prints Age ok, returns
              back in process: prints Processed
process(-4)   checkAge(-4): prints Bad age, then exit
              program over: no Processed, no Done

The output is Age ok, Processed, Bad age. If exit were replaced with return;, only checkAge would end, so Processed and Done would both print after Bad age.

The number in the parentheses is the exit code, passed to the operating system to report how the program ended:

  • 0, or the named constant EXIT_SUCCESS, means a normal end.
  • A nonzero value, or the named constant EXIT_FAILURE, means the program ended because of an error.

exit, EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE all come from <cstdlib>. Use exit sparingly: a program that can stop from anywhere is harder to follow. The return 0; at the end of main ends the program only because main is the function that was running everything.

Stubs and drivers: testing in pieces

A program with many functions is easier to build and debug one piece at a time. Two small tools help.

A stub is a dummy function that stands in for a function you have not written yet. It has the real header, so every call to it compiles, but its body is a placeholder. It usually prints a message showing it was called, and if it must return something, it returns a fixed value.

double shippingCost(double weight)     // stub
{
    cout << "shippingCost called with " << weight << endl;
    return 5.0;                        // fixed test value
}

With the stub in place, you can run and test main and the code that calls shippingCost, checking that it is called at the right time with the right argument. Later you replace the stub's body with the real calculation.

A driver works the other way round. It is a small throwaway program, or a main, whose only job is to call one function with chosen test values and show the results, so you can check that function on its own before it joins the full program.

bool isPassing(int score)     // the function being tested
{
    return score >= 60;
}

int main()                    // driver for isPassing
{
    cout << isPassing(59) << endl;    // expect 0
    cout << isPassing(60) << endl;    // expect 1
    cout << isPassing(100) << endl;   // expect 1
    return 0;
}

Good test values sit right on the edges, such as 59 and 60 here, because that is where mistakes like > instead of >= show up.

Memory aid: a stub is called by the program, sitting at the bottom waiting for calls. A driver does the calling: it drives the function being tested.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking two functions can differ only in return type. They cannot.
  • Thinking different parameter names make different functions. Names are not part of the signature.
  • Forgetting that 2.5 is a double and 'z' is a char when deciding which overload runs.
  • Writing a call that fits two overloads equally well, such as larger(3, 2.5).
  • Treating exit like return. exit ends the whole program, so nothing after it prints, anywhere.
  • Forgetting #include <cstdlib> for exit, EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE.
  • Swapping stub and driver. The stub replaces an unwritten function. The driver tests a written one.

What to remember for the test

  • Overloaded functions: same name, different parameter lists (number, types or order of types).
  • The compiler picks the version that matches the arguments. Exact matches win. Two equally good matches is an ambiguity error.
  • Signature = name + parameter types in order. Not the return type, not the parameter names.
  • Two functions that differ only in return type do not compile.
  • exit(n) from <cstdlib> ends the whole program at once, from any function. return ends only the current function.
  • 0 or EXIT_SUCCESS means a normal end. Nonzero or EXIT_FAILURE means an error.
  • Stub: dummy function with the real header, prints a message or returns a fixed value. It is called.
  • Driver: small program or main that calls one function with test values. It does the calling.
