Compiling each statement of the program separately
questions.explain:
Modular programming means dividing a program into small functions, each doing one task. The textbook also calls it divide and conquer: many small problems are easier to solve, test and fix than one huge one, and a function written once can be reused.

The other choices miss the idea. Putting everything inside `main` with comments between the parts is the opposite: it is still one big function. A global array of variables has nothing to do with splitting the work into functions. And compiling each statement separately is not how C++ programs are built, and it says nothing about how the program is organized.

questions.prompt: Identify lines A, B and C.
choices: A is a header, B is a prototype, C is a call
A is a prototype, B is a definition, C is a call
A is a call, B is a definition, C is a prototype
A is a prototype, B is a call, C is a definition
questions.explain:
Check two things on each line: does it start with a return type, and what follows the parentheses?
```
A  int cube(int n);          type in front, then ; and no body
B  int cube(int n) { ... }   type in front, then a body
C  x = cube(4);              no type in front, a value in ()
```
A is a prototype, B is a definition (header plus body on one line), and C is a call.

The tempting mistake is to call A a header. A header is the first line of a definition and never ends with a semicolon. Add the semicolon and leave out the body, and it becomes a prototype. C cannot be a prototype or a definition, because it has no return type in front.
questions.code:
int cube(int n);                        // A
int cube(int n) { return n * n * n; }   // B
x = cube(4);                            // C

questions.prompt: The header of a function definition ends with a semicolon, just like a prototype does.
A line such as `double avg(int, int);` that tells the compiler a function's name, return type and parameter types before the function is defined is called a function ____.
questions.explain: The answer is prototype, also called a function declaration. It is the function header with a semicolon added and no body. `double avg(int, int);` tells the compiler that `avg` takes two `int` values and returns a `double`. With that line near the top of the file, `main` can call `avg` even though the definition of `avg` comes further down.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Start in `main`. Each call jumps into the function, and when that function ends, control comes back to the statement right after the call, in the function that made it.
```
main  prints M1, then calls a
a     prints A1, then calls b
b     prints B1, then ends: back into a
a     prints A2, then ends: back into main
main  prints M2
```
So the output is M1, A1, B1, A2, M2, each on its own line. Two traps: `b` is defined first, but that does not make it run first, because a function runs only when it is called. And when `b` ends, control goes back to `a`, which still has A2 to print, not straight to `main`.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this program?
choices: A void function cannot be called from main
greet must be defined inside main
greet is called before the compiler has seen a prototype or definition for it
greet needs a return statement at the end
questions.explain:
The compiler reads the file from the top down. When it reaches `greet();` inside `main`, it has not yet seen anything named `greet`, so it reports an error such as "greet was not declared in this scope". The definition below `main` comes too late. Fix it by putting the prototype `void greet();` above `main`, or by moving the whole definition of `greet` above `main`.

The other choices state rules that do not exist. `main` can call a `void` function. A function can never be defined inside `main`. And a `void` function does not need a `return` statement.

questions.prompt: A function named grade receives a double and an int and returns a char. Which is its correct prototype?
choices: grade(double, int) : char;
void grade(double, int);
char grade(double x, int y)
char grade(double, int);
questions.explain:
Build a prototype in this order: return type, name, parameter types in parentheses, semicolon. This function returns a `char`, is named `grade`, and receives a `double` then an `int`. That gives `char grade(double, int);`.

`char grade(double x, int y)` has the right pieces but no semicolon, so it is a header, the first line of a definition, not a prototype. `void grade(double, int);` says the function returns nothing, but it returns a `char`. `grade(double, int) : char;` puts the return type at the end, which is not C++ syntax. In C++ the return type always comes first.

questions.prompt: Write the prototype for a function named isEven that receives one int and returns a bool. Leave out the parameter name and include the semicolon.
questions.explain: Put the pieces in order: return type `bool`, the name `isEven`, the parameter type `int` in parentheses, then a semicolon. That gives `bool isEven(int);`. A prototype only needs the parameter types, so the name can be left out, although `bool isEven(int n);` would also be legal. Without the final semicolon the line would be a header, not a prototype.

questions.prompt: Parameter names are optional in a function prototype.
questions.explain: True. The compiler uses a prototype only to check calls, so it needs the return type, the name, and the number and types of the parameters. Names add nothing to that check. `void show(int, double);` is a complete, legal prototype, and so is `void show(int count, double price);`. In the definition's header the names are required, because the body uses them.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Start in `main`. Each call to `line()` runs the body of `line` once, then control comes back to the next statement in `main`.
```
line();          prints ----
cout << "Menu"   prints Menu
line();          prints ---- again
```
So the output is three lines: ----, then Menu, then ----. Writing the definition of `line` above `main` does not make it run first. It runs only when it is called, and it is called twice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about function definitions is true?
choices: A function definition cannot appear inside the body of another function
Every function must be defined inside main to be callable
A void function must end with a return statement
Functions must be defined in the same order that they are called
questions.explain:
In C++ every function definition stands on its own at the top level of the file, outside all other functions. You cannot write one definition inside another function's body, not even inside `main`. Python allows a `def` inside a `def`, but C++ does not.

The other statements are false. Functions are defined outside `main`, not inside it. A `void` function may simply reach its closing brace, so it needs no `return`. And the order of the definitions does not have to match the order of the calls: with prototypes at the top, the definitions can come in any order.

questions.prompt: In a program that has several functions, where does execution begin?
choices: At the first function defined in the file
At the first statement of main
At the first prototype
At the function with the longest body
questions.explain: A C++ program always starts at the first statement of `main`, wherever `main` is placed in the file. Functions defined above `main` do not run first. They wait until a call reaches them. A prototype only announces a function, so it runs nothing. And the length of a function's body has nothing to do with where the program starts.

questions.prompt: In the code shown, which statement is correct?
choices: n is an argument and 7 is a parameter
Both n and 7 are parameters
n is a parameter and 7 is an argument
Both n and 7 are arguments
questions.explain:
In `void show(int n)`, `n` is declared in the function header, so it is a parameter: a variable waiting to receive a value. In `show(7)`, the 7 is written in the call, so it is an argument: the value being sent. When the call runs, `n` is created holding 7.

Saying `n` is the argument and 7 the parameter swaps the two words. Calling both of them parameters, or both arguments, ignores where each one is written: one in the header, one in the call. Memory aid: the parameter is the placeholder in the definition, the argument is the actual value at the call.

questions.prompt: A variable listed in the parentheses of a function header that receives data from the caller is called a ____.
questions.explain: The term is parameter. It is a variable declared inside the parentheses of a function header, such as `n` in `void show(int n)`. When the function is called, the parameter is created and given a copy of the argument's value, so `show(7)` starts the body with `n` equal to 7. It is also called a formal parameter or formal argument. The value written in the call is the argument.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
There are two separate variables named `n`, one in `main` and one in `bump`.
```
main          n = 5
bump(n)       bump's n is created as a copy: 5
n = n + 10    bump's n is 15, main's n is still 5
cout          prints 15
bump ends     bump's n is destroyed
cout in main  prints main's n: 5
```
So the output is 15, then 5. Passing by value copies the value, and nothing done to the copy reaches `main`. The tempting wrong answer, 15 and 15, assumes that the same name means the same variable. It never does across two functions.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Arguments go into parameters by position, and each value is converted to its parameter's type.
```
show(3.9, 4)   a = 3.9 converted to int: 3 (fraction dropped)
               b = 4 converted to double: 4.0
               prints 3 4      (cout shows 4.0 as 4)
show(4, 3.5)   a = 4, b = 3.5
               prints 4 3.5
```
So the output is `3 4`, then `4 3.5`. Two traps: double to int drops the fraction, it does not round, so 3.9 becomes 3, not 4. And `cout` prints a whole-number double without a decimal point, so 4.0 appears as 4.

questions.prompt: Given the prototype void box(int w, int h, char c); which call is legal?
choices: box(int 2, int 3, '*');
questions.explain:
`box` has three parameters, an `int`, an `int` and a `char`. A legal call passes exactly three values, in that order, with no types: `box(2, 3, '*');`.

`box(2, 3);` has too few arguments. Nothing gives the third parameter a value, because it has no default, so it does not compile. `box(2, 3, '*', 1);` has one argument too many. `box(int 2, int 3, '*');` writes types in the call, which is never allowed: types belong in headers and prototypes only.

questions.prompt: The call show(x * 2 + 1); is legal for a function with one int parameter, where x is an int.
questions.explain: True. An argument can be any expression whose value suits the parameter's type. C++ works out `x * 2 + 1` first and copies only the result into the parameter. If `x` is 4, the call behaves exactly like `show(9);`: the parameter starts out holding 9.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`swapIt` has value parameters, so `a` and `b` are copies of `x` and `y`.
```
main          x = 1, y = 2
swapIt(x, y)  a = 1, b = 2   (copies)
t = a         t = 1
a = b         a = 2
b = t         b = 1          the copies are swapped
swapIt ends   a, b, t destroyed
main          x = 1, y = 2   untouched
```
The output is `1 2`. The swap worked, but only on the copies. To swap the caller's variables, the parameters must be reference parameters, `int& a, int& b`, which a later lesson covers.

questions.prompt: An argument of type double is passed to an int parameter. What happens?
choices: It is converted to int and the fractional part is discarded
The program does not compile
The parameter becomes a double for that call
The value is rounded to the nearest integer
questions.explain:
C++ converts the argument to the parameter's type, just as `int n = 3.9;` would. Converting a double to an int drops the fractional part, so 3.9 becomes 3 and -3.9 becomes -3.

Why the others are wrong: it does not round, so 3.9 does not become 4. The program does compile, because this conversion is legal even though it loses information. And the parameter never changes type for one call: the header says `int`, so it is always an `int`.

questions.prompt: If a function has two parameters and no default arguments, a call with one argument is legal.
questions.explain: False. A call must supply one argument for every parameter, matched left to right. With two parameters and only one argument, the second parameter has nothing to copy, and the compiler reports an error such as "too few arguments to function". The only exception is a parameter that has a default argument, a value written into the header for use when the caller leaves it out. This function has none.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
A `char` is stored as a number code, and in arithmetic C++ uses that code.
```
show('*', 3)       c = '*', n = 3     prints ***
show('a' + 1, 2)   'a' + 1 is 97 + 1, the int 98
                   c is a char, so 98 becomes 'b'
                   n = 2              prints bb
```
So the output is `***`, then `bb`. The parameter's type decides what arrives: `c` is a `char`, so the int 98 is converted to the character with code 98, and `cout` prints a char as a letter. The tempting wrong answer has 98 in it. That is what you would get if `c` were an `int`: the second line would then be 9898.

questions.prompt: How many values can a function send back to its caller using a return statement?
choices: Any number, separated by commas
One
Two
As many as it has parameters
questions.explain: One. A `return` statement sends back exactly one value, and the moment it runs the function is over, so there is no chance to send a second one. A function may contain several `return` statements, for example one in an if and one after it, but each call runs only one of them. Writing `return x, y;` does not send two values: it compiles, but only `y` is sent back. The number of parameters has nothing to do with it. To give back two or more results, a function uses reference parameters, covered in a later lesson.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this function?
choices: Nothing, it is correct
The parameter n must be a reference
A void function cannot return a value; the return type should be int
The expression n * n * n needs parentheses
questions.explain:
The header says `void`, which means the function returns no value, but the body tries to `return n * n * n;`. That is a compile error: a `void` function may only use `return;` with no value. The function computes a cube, so the fix is to make the return type `int`: `int cube(int n)`.

The other choices are wrong. The code is not correct as written. The parameter does not need to be a reference, because the function only reads `n`. And `n * n * n` needs no parentheses.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
A call to a value-returning function is replaced by the value it returns, so it can sit inside arithmetic or inside another call.
```
sq(3) + sq(4)   9 + 16 = 25
sq(sq(2))       inner call first: sq(2) is 4
                then the outer call: sq(4) is 16
```
So the output is 25, then 16. For a call inside a call, always work from the inside out: the inner result becomes the argument of the outer call.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
A `return;` in a `void` function ends the function right there, even when statements remain below it.
```
check(-1)   n < 0 is true: prints neg
            return; ends check, so ok is not printed
check(2)    n < 0 is false: the if block is skipped
            prints ok
```
So the output is neg, then ok. The tempting wrong answer prints ok after neg as well, forgetting that `return;` stops the function before its last line.

questions.prompt: A void function may contain the statement return; with no value.
questions.explain: True. `return;` with no value is how a `void` function leaves early, for example as soon as it detects bad input. Control goes straight back to the caller. What a `void` function may not do is return a value: `return 0;` inside a `void` function is a compile error.

questions.prompt: Write the header (no semicolon) of a function named larger that receives two ints named a and b and returns an int.
questions.explain: Write the return type, then the name, then each parameter with its own type, and no semicolon: `int larger(int a, int b)`. A common slip is `int larger(int a, b)`, which does not compile because every parameter needs its own type. Adding a semicolon would turn the line into a prototype, which is not what was asked.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`isOdd` returns the value of the comparison `n % 2 != 0`, which is a `bool`.
```
isOdd(7)   7 % 2 is 1, and 1 != 0 is true    cout prints 1
isOdd(8)   8 % 2 is 0, and 0 != 0 is false   cout prints 0
```
`cout` prints `true` as 1 and `false` as 0, not as words, and nothing separates the two values. So the output is `10`.

questions.prompt: isPrime is a function with one int parameter that returns bool. Which if statement is correct?
choices: if (isPrime)
if (bool isPrime(n))
if (isPrime(int n))
if (isPrime(n))
questions.explain:
To use the answer, the function must be called: its name, then the argument in parentheses, with no types. `if (isPrime(n))` calls `isPrime` with `n`, and the `bool` it returns becomes the condition.

`if (isPrime)` names the function without calling it. No argument is passed and the function never runs. C++ treats a function's name in a condition as true, so this test is always true, and g++ only warns. `if (isPrime(int n))` and `if (bool isPrime(n))` write types inside a call, and neither compiles.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Two conversions happen, one on the way in and one on the way out.
```
half(7)          the int 7 becomes the double 7.0
x / 2            7.0 / 2 is 3.5, returned as a double
int a = 3.5      an int cannot hold a fraction: a is 3
double b = 3.5   b is 3.5
```
The output is `3 3.5`. The function returns 3.5 both times. What differs is the variable that receives it. The int truncates, so `a` is 3, not 4.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Inside `avg`, `a`, `b` and 2 are all `int`, so the division is integer division.
```
(a + b) / 2   (3 + 4) / 2 is 7 / 2, which is 3 (fraction dropped)
return 3      converted to the return type: 3.0
cout          prints a whole-number double as 3
```
The output is `3`, not 3.5. The `double` return type comes too late: the fraction was already lost in the division. Writing `(a + b) / 2.0` makes it a double division, and then the function returns 3.5.

questions.prompt: What happens when a return statement executes inside a value-returning function?
choices: The function ends at once and the value goes back to the caller
The value is stored and the function keeps running to its closing brace
The whole program ends
The value is printed on the screen
questions.explain:
When `return` runs, the function ends at once, and the value goes back to the place where the function was called, where it replaces the call. Statements after the `return` are skipped.

The other choices are wrong. The function does not keep running to its closing brace. The program does not end: only the current function does, and the caller carries on. And nothing is printed: a returned value reaches the screen only if the caller sends it to `cout`.

questions.prompt: Where can a local variable defined inside a function be used?
choices: In any function in the file
Only inside that function
In main and in the function that defined it
Anywhere after the function is first called
questions.explain:
A local variable can be used only inside the function that defines it. That part of the program is its scope. Any other function, `main` included, that tries to use the name gets a "not declared in this scope" error.

The other choices all give it a wider scope than it has. It is not visible in every function, it is not shared with `main`, and calling the function does not make the name available anywhere else. To share a value, pass it as an argument or return it.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
There are two variables named `total`. Inside `f`, `int total = 5;` has a type in front, so it defines a new local that shadows the global.
```
start         global total = 100
f() begins    local total = 5    (the global is hidden in f)
total++       local total = 6
cout in f     prints 6
f returns     the local is destroyed
cout in main  prints the global: 100
```
So the output is 6, then 100. The tempting wrong answer is 6 and 6, which treats `int total = 5;` as a change to the global. Without the `int`, it would have been.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`calls` is a static local, so it is created and set to 0 only once, and it keeps its value between calls.
```
1st tick()   calls = 0 (initialized now), calls++ gives 1, prints 1
2nd tick()   initializer skipped, calls is 1, ++ gives 2, prints 2
3rd tick()   calls is 2, ++ gives 3, prints 3
```
So the output is 1, 2, 3. Without `static`, `calls` would be re-created at 0 on every call, and the program would print 1 three times.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`a` is an ordinary local and `b` is a static local. Track both across the three calls.
```
call   a at start   b at start          after ++   prints
1st    0 (new)      0 (initialized)     a=1 b=1    11
2nd    0 (new)      1 (kept)            a=1 b=2    12
3rd    0 (new)      2 (kept)            a=1 b=3    13
```
`a` is born at 0 every call, so it always prints 1. `b` is set to 0 only on the first call and keeps counting. There is no space between the two values, so the lines are 11, 12, 13.

questions.prompt: Which C++ keyword makes a local variable keep its value between calls to its function?
questions.explain: The key word is `static`. Writing `static int calls = 0;` inside a function makes `calls` live for the whole run of the program, so it keeps its value from one call to the next. It is initialized only once, the first time its definition is reached. Its scope does not grow: only that function can use the name.

questions.prompt: A local int variable that is defined without an initial value is automatically set to 0.
questions.explain: False. An ordinary local such as `int sum;` is not set to anything. It holds garbage: an unpredictable leftover value from whatever used that memory before. Reading it before assigning a value is a bug. Only global variables and static locals are set to 0 automatically. That is why locals should always be initialized, as in `int sum = 0;`.

questions.prompt: A global int variable that is not explicitly initialized starts out as 0.
questions.explain: True. A global variable that is defined with no value, such as `int hits;` outside every function, is set to 0 before `main` starts. The same is true of static locals. Only ordinary locals start with garbage.

questions.prompt: Why are global variables generally discouraged?
choices: They are slower than local variables by a factor of ten
They cannot be used inside functions
Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace and functions become hard to reuse
They must always be declared const
questions.explain:
Any function can change a global, so when a global holds a wrong value, the bug could be in any function that touches it. Functions that depend on a global are also hard to reuse in another program, and hard to test on their own. Passing data through parameters and return values keeps each function self-contained.

The other reasons are false. Globals are not ten times slower. They can be used inside functions, and that is the whole problem. And they do not have to be `const`, although making a global `const` does remove the danger.

questions.prompt: Why is a global constant such as const double TAX_RATE = 0.07; usually acceptable?
choices: Constants take no memory
Constants are local to main
Global constants may be modified by any function
No function can accidentally change its value
questions.explain:
The danger with a global is that any function can change it when it should not. A constant cannot be changed at all: a function that tries `TAX_RATE = 0.5;` gets a compile error. So every function can safely read the shared value.

The other choices are false. A constant still takes memory. A constant defined outside all functions is global, not local to `main`. And the claim that global constants may be modified by any function is the opposite of the truth.

questions.prompt: What is the error?
choices: x is local to first, so second cannot use it
first must return x
x must be a static variable
second needs a prototype before it can use x
questions.explain:
`x` is defined inside `first`, so its scope is `first` only. `second` cannot see it, and the compiler reports that `x` was not declared in this scope. `second` would need its own `x`, or to receive the value as a parameter.

The other fixes do not help. Returning `x` from `first` would not let `second` use the name `x`. Making `x` static changes its lifetime, not its scope, so other functions still cannot use it. And a prototype tells the compiler about a function, not about another function's variables.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`level` is a global, and `up` has no local named `level`, so `level = level * 2;` changes the global itself. Every call doubles it, and the changes last.
```
start     level = 1
up()      level = 2
up()      level = 4
up()      level = 8
```
`main` prints 8. If `up` had defined its own local, as in `int level = 1;`, and doubled that, only the local would change, and `main` would print 1.

questions.prompt: The initializer in static int n = 10; runs every time the function is called.
questions.explain: False. A static local is created and initialized only once, the first time execution reaches its definition. On every later call the line `static int n = 10;` is skipped, and `n` keeps whatever value it had at the end of the previous call. That is the whole point of `static`. An ordinary local, `int n = 10;`, would be set to 10 on every call.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the lifetime of an ordinary local variable?
choices: It exists for the whole run of the program
It comes into being on entry to the function and is destroyed on return
It is created when the program starts and destroyed when main ends
It is created at the first call and keeps its value for later calls
questions.explain:
An ordinary local comes into being when its function runs and is thrown away as soon as the function returns. The next call gets a brand-new variable. That is why an ordinary local cannot remember anything between calls.

The other choices describe other kinds of variable. Existing for the whole run is true of globals and static locals. Being created when the program starts is how globals behave. And being created at the first call and keeping its value afterwards describes a static local.

questions.prompt: Where should a default argument be specified when a prototype is used?
choices: In both the prototype and the header
In the header only
In the call only
In the prototype only
questions.explain:
In the prototype only. When a program has a prototype, the default goes there, because the prototype is what the compiler has already read when it checks the calls in `main`. The definition's header then leaves the default out.

Putting it in both is a compile error, even when the two values match. Putting it in the header only does not work either: a call such as `pay(40)` in `main` is checked against the prototype, which demands every argument, so the compiler reports too few arguments. And a call never holds a default: it simply leaves the argument out.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this prototype?
choices: Once a parameter has a default, all parameters to its right must have defaults
A prototype cannot have default arguments
Default arguments must be 0
There can be only one default argument per function
questions.explain:
Defaults must sit at the right-hand end of the parameter list. Once a parameter has a default, every parameter to its right must have one too. Here `a` has a default but `b`, to its right, does not, so the prototype does not compile. The reason is that arguments fill parameters from the left, so a caller could never leave out `a` and still give `b` a value.

The other choices are false. Prototypes are exactly where defaults usually go. A default does not have to be 0. And a function may have several defaults, as long as they are all at the right end.
questions.code: void pack(int a = 1, int b, int c = 3);

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Arguments fill the parameters from the left, and any parameter left over takes its default.
```
show(1)         a=1, b=10 (default), c=100 (default)   111
show(1, 2)      a=1, b=2, c=100 (default)              103
show(1, 2, 3)   a=1, b=2, c=3, no defaults used        6
```
So the output is 111, 103, 6. A default is used only when its argument is missing. Once the call supplies a value, the default for that parameter is ignored.

questions.prompt: Given void f(int a, int b = 2, int c = 3); which call is illegal?
questions.explain:
`a` has no default, so every call must supply at least one argument, for `a`. `f();` supplies nothing, so it does not compile ("too few arguments").

The others are legal. `f(5)` fills `a` and uses both defaults, so b = 2 and c = 3. `f(5, 6)` uses only the default for `c`. `f(5, 6, 7)` uses no defaults. A caller may leave arguments off the end, but only ones that have defaults.

questions.prompt: Which symbol, placed after the type in a parameter, makes it a reference parameter?
questions.explain: The symbol is the ampersand, `&`. Written after the type in a parameter, as in `void doubleIt(int& n)`, it makes `n` a reference parameter: another name for the caller's variable, not a copy. So `n = n * 2;` inside the function doubles the caller's variable. `int &n` and `int & n` mean the same thing.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Both parameters have `&`, so `a` is another name for `x` and `b` is another name for `y`. No copies are made.
```
start    x = 1, y = 2
t = a    t = 1          (a is x)
a = b    x = 2          (b is y)
b = t    y = 1
```
The output is `2 1`. Without the two ampersands, the same body would swap only copies and the program would print `1 2`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`a` is a value parameter, so it holds a copy of `x`. `b` is a reference parameter, so it is another name for `y`.
```
start     x = 1, y = 1
a += 5    the copy a is 6, x is still 1
b += 5    b is y, so y is 6
```
After the call `x` is 1 and `y` is 6, so the output is `1 6`. Each parameter is judged on its own: only the one with `&` can change the caller's variable.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this program?
choices: inc must return a value
The function name inc is reserved
A literal such as 5 cannot be passed to a reference parameter; it needs a variable
The parameter must be const
questions.explain:
A reference parameter is another name for a variable in the caller, and this function changes it with `n++`. The literal 5 is not a variable: there is nothing for `n` to be another name for, and nothing that could be increased. So `inc(5)` does not compile. Pass a variable instead: `int k = 5; inc(k);` leaves `k` at 6.

The other choices are wrong. `inc` is `void`, so it need not return a value. `inc` is an ordinary name. And making the parameter `const` would forbid the function from changing `n`, so `n++` would stop compiling.

questions.prompt: Write the prototype for a function named order that receives two int reference parameters and returns nothing. Leave out the parameter names.
questions.explain: Return type `void` because it returns nothing, the name `order`, then `int&` for each parameter, then a semicolon: `void order(int&, int&);`. In a prototype the parameter names may be left out, but the ampersands may not. `void order(int, int);` would declare value parameters, which would not match a header such as `void order(int& a, int& b)`.

questions.prompt: A reference parameter is another name for the argument variable in the caller.
questions.explain: True. A reference parameter makes no copy. It is a second name for the variable the caller passed: one box in memory with two names on it. So when the function changes the parameter, it changes the caller's variable. That is what makes a working swap function possible.

questions.prompt: Which header suits a function that must give both the quotient and the remainder of two ints back to the caller?
choices: int divide(int a, int b, int q, int r)
void divide(int& a, int& b, int q, int r)
int divide(int a, int b)
void divide(int a, int b, int& q, int& r)
questions.explain:
Two results must go back, but `return` can send only one value. So the two result variables are passed by reference: `void divide(int a, int b, int& q, int& r)`. The inputs `a` and `b` are only read, so they are value parameters. `q` and `r` have `&`, so the function can store the quotient and remainder straight into the caller's variables.

`int divide(int a, int b)` can return only one of the two results. `int divide(int a, int b, int q, int r)` makes `q` and `r` copies, so whatever is stored in them is lost. `void divide(int& a, int& b, int q, int r)` puts the ampersands on the wrong parameters: the results are still copies.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`total` is another name for `t`, and `amount` defaults to 1 when it is left out.
```
start         t = 0
addTo(t)      amount = 1 (default)   t = 0 + 1 = 1
addTo(t, 5)   amount = 5             t = 1 + 5 = 6
addTo(t)      amount = 1 (default)   t = 6 + 1 = 7
```
The output is `7`. Every call changes `t` itself, because `total` is a reference. A reference parameter and a default argument work fine together, as long as the defaulted parameter comes last.

questions.prompt: The declarations int &x and int& x mean the same thing.
questions.explain: True. Spaces around the `&` do not matter: `int& x`, `int &x` and `int & x` all make `x` a reference to an `int`. What does matter is the order. The `&` must come after the type and before the name, so `int x&` is an error.

questions.prompt: What lets the compiler distinguish overloaded functions?
choices: Different numbers or types of parameters
Different return types
Different parameter names
Different function body lengths
questions.explain:
The compiler tells overloaded functions apart by their parameter lists: how many parameters each has, their types, and their order. At each call it looks at the arguments and picks the version whose parameter list matches.

A different return type is not enough, because a call such as `getValue()` says nothing about which return type you want, so two functions that differ only that way do not compile. Parameter names do not count, since a call never mentions them. And the length of a body plays no part.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Three functions share the name `show`, and each call picks the one whose parameter type matches its argument.
```
show(5)     5 is an int        show(int)     prints int 5
show(2.5)   2.5 is a double    show(double)  prints double 2.5
show('z')   'z' is a char      show(char)    prints char z
```
So the output is int 5, double 2.5, char z, on three lines. A number with a decimal point is a `double`, and single quotes make a `char`. Every call matches one version exactly, so no conversion happens.

questions.prompt: Calling the exit function, for example `exit(0);`, ends the whole program immediately, even when it is called from a function other than main.
questions.explain: True. `exit`, from `<cstdlib>`, ends the entire program the moment it runs, no matter which function calls it or how deeply the calls are nested. Nothing else runs: not the rest of that function, and not the rest of `main`. Compare `return`, which ends only the current function and sends control back to its caller.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Follow the calls until `exit` runs.
```
main   prints 1, then calls stop
stop   prints A
stop   exit(0): the whole program ends here
```
So the output is 1, then A. `cout << "B"` never runs, because it comes after `exit` in `stop`. And control never goes back to `main`, so 2 is not printed either. The tempting wrong answer, 1, A, 2, treats `exit` like `return`. A `return` would have gone back to `main`, which would then print 2.

questions.prompt: A dummy function with the correct header that stands in for a function not yet written, used for testing, is called a ____.
questions.explain: The term is stub. A stub has the real function's header but a placeholder body. Usually it just prints a message such as "calcTax called", or returns a fixed value. It lets you test the rest of the program, the code that calls the function, before the real function is written. Later the stub's body is replaced with the real code.

questions.prompt: What is a driver?
choices: A function that replaces one that has not been written
A function that calls exit
A small program or main that calls a function with test values to check it
A prototype with default arguments
questions.explain:
A driver is a small program, or a `main`, whose only job is to call one function with chosen test values and show the results, so that function can be checked on its own.

A function that stands in for one not yet written is a stub, the opposite tool: the stub is called by the program, while the driver does the calling. A driver has nothing to do with `exit`. And a prototype with default arguments is just a declaration, not a testing tool.

questions.prompt: The first line of a function definition, which gives the return type, the name and the parameter list, is called the function ____.
questions.explain: The answer is the function header: the first line of a definition, holding the return type, the name and the parameter list, such as `double area(double w, double h)`. The body in braces comes right after it, with no semicolon in between. Add a semicolon and leave out the body, and the same text becomes a prototype instead.

questions.prompt: Which line is a function call, rather than a function header or a prototype?
choices: void printTotal(int amount)
void printTotal(int);
printTotal(sales);
void printTotal(int amount);
questions.explain:
`printTotal(sales);` is the call: just the function name and the value to send, with no return type and no types in the parentheses.

The other three lines all start with the return type `void`, so none of them can be a call. `void printTotal(int amount)` has no semicolon, so it is a header, the first line of a definition. `void printTotal(int);` and `void printTotal(int amount);` both end with a semicolon, so both are prototypes. One has a parameter name and one does not, and both forms are legal.

questions.prompt: Writing the statements for a task once, as a function, and then calling that function wherever the task is needed is a benefit the textbook calls code ____.
questions.explain: The term is code reuse. Instead of copying the same statements into every place a task is needed, you write them once inside a function and call the function each time. For example, a `printHeading()` function can be called at the top of five different reports. If the heading has to change, you change it in one place. Divide and conquer is the related idea of splitting a big program into small functions.

questions.prompt: When a function finishes, control always goes back to main, no matter which function called it.
questions.explain: False. A function returns to the statement right after its call, in the function that made the call. If `main` calls `a` and `a` calls `b`, then when `b` ends, control goes back into `a`, which runs its remaining statements. Only when `a` ends does control return to `main`. Control goes straight back to `main` only when `main` made the call.

questions.prompt: A program has the function `void showValue(int quantity)`. Write a statement that calls it and passes the int variable count.
questions.explain: A call is the function name with the argument in parentheses: `showValue(count);`. Do not write a type: `showValue(int count);` does not compile, because types belong in headers and prototypes, never in calls. And do not use the parameter name: `quantity` is the name used inside the function, and it receives the value of `count` when the call runs.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Arguments are copied into parameters by position: first to first, second to second. The parameter names `big` and `small` do not make C++ check which value is bigger.
```
showDiff(b, a)   big = 10, small = 3    prints 10 - 3 = 7
showDiff(a, b)   big = 3,  small = 10   prints 3 - 10 = -7
```
So the output is 7, then -7. The trap is to assume the larger number lands in `big` both times. Whatever is written first in the call goes into the first parameter.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this function?
choices: Each parameter needs its own data type: int x, int y, int z
Parameters must be separated by semicolons, not commas
A function cannot have more than two parameters
The return expression must be in parentheses
questions.explain:
In a parameter list every parameter needs its own type. Ordinary variable definitions let one type cover several names, as in `int x, y, z;`, but a parameter list does not, so `y` and `z` are errors. The fix is `int addAll(int x, int y, int z)`.

The other choices are false: parameters are separated by commas, not semicolons, a function may have as many parameters as it needs, and a return expression does not need parentheses.

questions.prompt: After a function returns, main can still use that function's parameter variables.
questions.explain: False. A parameter exists only while its function runs. It is created when the call starts, filled with a copy of the argument, and destroyed when the function returns. Its scope, the part of the program where its name can be used, is the body of its own function. If `main` used that name, the compiler would report that it was not declared in this scope. To get a result out of a function, return it or use a reference parameter.

questions.prompt: You are writing a function that receives a variable from the caller, and you must be sure the function cannot change the caller's variable. What should you do?
choices: Make the parameter a reference parameter with &
Pass the argument by value, using an ordinary parameter with no &
Make the variable global
Give the parameter the same name as the caller's variable
questions.explain:
Pass by value, using an ordinary parameter with no `&`. The parameter is then a separate copy in its own memory, so whatever the function does to it, the caller's variable is safe.

Why the others fail: a reference parameter with `&` is the opposite tool, because it is exactly how a function is allowed to change the caller's variable. Making the variable global, defined outside every function, lets every function change it, which removes protection. Giving the parameter the same name as the caller's variable does nothing: they are still two separate variables.

questions.prompt: In the code below, x is still 5 after the call, because the parameter is an independent copy of the argument. The call is made by ___ (one word).
questions.explain: The answer is value: `x` is passed by value. When `bump(x)` runs, the parameter `n` is a new variable holding a copy of 5. `n++` makes the copy 6, and the copy is destroyed when `bump` ends. `x` sits in a different memory location, so it is still 5 and the program prints 5. Pass by value is what C++ does for every parameter written without `&`.

questions.prompt: The user types 2, then 5, then 1, then 3. What does this print?
questions.explain:
This is the menu-driven pattern: a loop reads a choice and a `switch` calls one function for that choice. `n` is 6 throughout.
```
reads 2   case 2: showSquare(6)   prints 36
reads 5   no case 5, so default   prints ?
reads 1   case 1: showDouble(6)   prints 12
reads 3   case 3: break           prints nothing
          choice != 3 is false, so the loop ends
```
The output is 36, ?, 12 on three lines. A `break` inside a `switch` leaves only the `switch`, not the loop. The loop stops because its condition becomes false after the 3.

questions.prompt: When a program is designed with functions, what does a hierarchy chart show?
choices: The order in which every statement runs, with decision diamonds
The value of every variable at each step
How the variables are laid out in memory
Which functions call which other functions
questions.explain:
A hierarchy chart shows which functions call which other functions. It is a tree of boxes: `main` at the top and, under each function, the functions it calls. It shows the structure of the program.

It does not show the order of statements or decision diamonds: that is a flowchart, which shows step-by-step logic. It does not record variable values at each step, which is what a trace table does. And it says nothing about how variables are laid out in memory.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
The header says `int half`, so whatever the `return` produces is converted to `int` before it leaves the function.
```
half(7.0)   7.0 / 2 is 3.5, returned as the int 3
double d    d = 3, which is 3.0, printed as 3
half(9.8)   9.8 / 2 is 4.9, returned as the int 4
```
So the output is 3, then 4. Storing the result in a `double` cannot bring the .5 back, because it was lost inside the function. The conversion truncates, so 4.9 becomes 4, not 5.

questions.prompt: Which choice describes every problem in this function?
choices: It has no return statement; the arithmetic is correct
result must be an int because the parameters are ints
It has no return statement, and only c is divided by 3 (with integer division)
Only the arithmetic is wrong; a double function may end without return
questions.explain:
There are two problems. First, the function promises a `double` but never runs a `return`, so it reaches its closing brace with no value to hand back. g++ only warns, but the result the caller gets is undefined. Second, `/` is done before `+`, so `a + b + c / 3` means `a + b + (c / 3)`, and `c / 3` is integer division. The fix for both:
```
return (a + b + c) / 3.0;
```
The other choices are wrong. The arithmetic is not correct. `result` may be a `double` even though the parameters are `int`. And a `double` function may not end without a `return`.

questions.prompt: Functions that send a value back to the statement that called them, such as pow, are called ____ functions.
questions.explain: The term is value-returning function: a function whose header names a return type other than `void` and which sends one value back with `return`. `pow` is one: `pow(2.0, 3.0)` is replaced by 8, which the caller can store or print. A `void` function is the other kind: it does a job and sends nothing back.

questions.prompt: A program contains `int cube(int num)`, which returns num cubed. Write one statement that passes 4 to cube and stores the returned value in the existing int variable result.
questions.explain: Put the call on the right side of the assignment: `result = cube(4);`. The call runs first and returns 64, the value replaces the call, and `=` stores 64 in `result`. Do not put `int` in front, because `result` already exists. And `cube(4);` on its own would compute 64 and throw it away.

questions.prompt: A function defines a local `int total;` while a global `int total;` also exists. Inside that function, the local one ____ the global one (one word).
questions.explain: The word is shadows (hides also works). When a function defines a local with the same name as a global, every use of that name inside the function means the local, and the global is hidden there. For example, with a global `int total = 100;`, a function containing `int total = 5; total++;` changes only its local, and the global stays 100. Outside that function, `total` means the global again.

questions.prompt: This function compiles.
questions.explain: False. The parameter `n` belongs to the function's body, so `int n = 2;` tries to define a second variable named `n` in the same place. g++ reports "declaration of int n shadows a parameter". To change the parameter's value, assign without a type: `n = 2;`. Different functions may each have their own `n`, because each one's scope is its own function.

questions.prompt: What happens with this program?
choices: It prints 100
Compile error: getBonus uses bonus before bonus is defined
It prints 0, because globals start at 0
It prints an unpredictable value
questions.explain:
A global's scope runs from its definition to the end of the file, and the compiler reads from the top down. `getBonus` uses `bonus` before the line `int bonus = 50;`, so at that point the name is unknown and the program does not compile.

The program never runs, so it cannot print anything. It would print 100 if `int bonus = 50;` were moved above `getBonus`. The zero rule only applies to a global with no initial value, and it does not help a function that cannot see the global.

questions.prompt: A static local int that is defined without an initial value starts out holding garbage, just like an ordinary local int.
questions.explain: False. A static local is set to 0 automatically when it has no initial value, just like a global. So `static int s;` starts at 0: if a function prints `s` and then adds 1, its first two calls print 0 and then 1. Only ordinary locals start with garbage.

questions.prompt: The period during which a variable exists in memory, from when it is created until it is destroyed, is called its ____.
questions.explain: The word is lifetime: how long a variable exists in memory, from creation to destruction. An ordinary local lives for one call of its function. A global or a static local lives for the whole run. Do not confuse it with scope, which is where in the program the name can be used. A static local has a small scope (one function) but a long lifetime (the whole run).

questions.prompt: Given `void f(int a = 1, int b = 2, int c = 3);`, a call may leave out the argument for b and still supply one for c, as in `f(5, , 7);`.
questions.explain: False. Arguments fill parameters from the left, and a call cannot leave a gap, so `f(5, , 7);` is a syntax error. Only arguments at the end can be left out: `f()`, `f(5)`, `f(5, 6)` and `f(5, 6, 7)` are the legal forms. To give `c` the value 7, you must also give `b` a value, as in `f(5, 2, 7)`.

questions.prompt: LIMIT is a global `const int`. Which prototype is illegal?
choices: void f(int a, int b = 10);
void f(int a, int b = LIMIT);
void f(int a, int b = LIMIT * 2);
void f(int a, int b = a);
questions.explain:
A default argument may not use another parameter of the same function, so `void f(int a, int b = a);` is illegal. g++ reports that parameter `a` may not appear in this context.

The other three are legal. A literal such as 10 is the most common kind of default. A named constant such as `LIMIT` is fine. And an expression built from constants, such as `LIMIT * 2`, is fine too.

questions.prompt: This function is meant to store the user's input in the caller's variable. What is wrong with it?
choices: The & belongs after the type (int &count), and it is not written when the variable is used (cin >> count)
Nothing; the & may go on either side of the name
A void function cannot read input with cin
The & must also be written in every call, as in readCount(&n)
questions.explain:
Two things are wrong. In a declaration the `&` goes after the type and before the name: `int& count` or `int &count`, never `int count&`. And once the parameter is declared, it is used like any other variable, with no `&`: `cin >> count;`. Fixed that way, the input goes straight into the caller's variable.

The other choices are wrong. The `&` cannot go after the name. A `void` function can use `cin` like any other function. And the call has no `&`: you write `readCount(n);`. `&n` in a call means the address of `n`, a different thing that does not compile here.

questions.prompt: For a reference parameter, the & appears in both the prototype and the function header, but not in the function call.
questions.explain: True. The prototype and the header both describe the parameter, so both need the `&`: `void doubleIt(int&);` and `void doubleIt(int &n)`. The call only names the variable being passed: `doubleIt(x);`. It looks exactly like a call by value. You can tell a reference parameter only from the prototype or the header.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`a` is a reference, another name for the first argument. `b` is a copy of the second.
```
mix(p, q)   a is p, b = copy of q = 5
            a = a + b   p = 2 + 5 = 7
            b = 0       only the copy, q stays 5
            prints 7 5
mix(q, p)   a is q now, b = copy of p = 7
            a = a + b   q = 5 + 7 = 12
            b = 0       p stays 7
            prints 7 12
```
The output is `7 5`, then `7 12`. A reference parameter refers to whichever variable is passed in that call, so the second call changes `q`, not `p`.

questions.prompt: The user types 150, then 42. What does this print?
questions.explain:
`num` is a reference parameter, so it is another name for `main`'s `value`. Whatever `cin` stores in `num` lands in `value`.
```
cin >> num        value = 150
150 < 1 || 150 > 100   true: prints Out of range
cin >> num        value = 42
42 < 1 || 42 > 100     false: the loop ends
back in main      prints value * 2 = 84
```
The output is Out of range, then 84. If the parameter were `int num` without `&`, the numbers would go into a copy, `value` would stay 0, and `main` would print 0.

questions.prompt: A function's name together with the data types of its parameters, in order, is called the function's ____. C++ uses it to tell overloaded functions apart.
questions.explain: The term is signature: the function's name plus its parameter types, in order. For `double area(double w, double h)` the signature is `area(double, double)`. The return type and the parameter names are not part of it. Overloaded functions share a name, so they must have different signatures, which means different numbers, types or orders of parameters.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Both functions are named `area`, but one takes one `int` and the other takes two. The number of arguments decides which runs.
```
area(4)      one argument:  area(int side)               4 * 4 = 16
area(4, 6)   two arguments: area(int length, int width)  4 * 6 = 24
```
With the space printed between them, the output is `16 24`.

questions.prompt: Which header file must be included to use the exit function and the constants EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE?
choices: <iostream>
<cmath>
<cstdlib>
<exit>
questions.explain:
`exit`, `EXIT_SUCCESS` and `EXIT_FAILURE` all come from `<cstdlib>`, the C standard library header. `exit(0)` or `exit(EXIT_SUCCESS)` tells the operating system the program ended normally. A nonzero value or `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` reports an error.

The others are the wrong headers. `<iostream>` provides `cin` and `cout`. `<cmath>` provides math functions such as `pow` and `sqrt`. There is no standard header called `<exit>`.

questions.prompt: Two functions that are both named getValue and both take no parameters can be in the same program as long as one returns int and the other returns double.
questions.explain: False. Overloaded functions must differ in their parameter lists. These two both take no parameters, so both have the signature `getValue()`, and the program does not compile. A call `getValue()` would give the compiler nothing to choose by, because the return type is not part of the signature. To keep both, give them different names or different parameter lists.

questions.prompt: If a function does not return a value, the key word ____ is written as its return type.
questions.explain: The key word is `void`, meaning "no value". For example, `void printBanner()` prints something and sends nothing back. A `void` function ends at its closing brace, or earlier at `return;` with no value. Its call stands alone as a statement, `printBanner();`, because there is no value to store or print.

questions.prompt: Two different functions in the same program may each define a local variable named total.
questions.explain: True. A local variable's scope is only its own function, so a `total` in one function and a `total` in another are two separate variables in separate memory. Changing one never touches the other. What is not allowed is two variables that share a name inside one block of a function.
